procedural_history.originating_court: High Court of Judicature at Calcutta
procedural_history.impugned_order: Interim order dated 30.4.2015 passed in M.P. no. I of 2015 in Suo-motu Writ Petition (unnumbered) of 2015.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court initiated a process for selection and appointment of Junior Divisional Judicial Officers. Justice C.S. Karnan purportedly in exercise of suo-motu extra ordinary original jurisdiction (under Article 226 of the Constitution of India, read with Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure), passed an order dated 10.3.2017 to register a case against two Judges of the Supreme Court. The High Court also initiated Suo Motu Contempt A Petition (Civil) No. I of 2017 against Justice Karnan.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Registrar General filed a petition which was assigned Special Leave Petition (Civil) no. 14842 of 2015. The Supreme Court granted permission to file a special leave petition and issued notice. The Supreme Court stayed the interim order dated 30.4.2015 passed by the High Court. The Supreme Court ordered that there shall not be any interference by any person/authority or learned Judges in completing the process initiated by the High Court for selection and appointment of Junior Divisional Judicial Officers until the disposal of the special leave petition. The Supreme Court was approached because Justice Karnan sent representations to various Govt. Authorities regarding high court judges and passed orders against Supreme Court judges.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court has the jurisdiction to initiate contempt proceedings against a sitting High Court Judge.

facts: A sitting High Court Judge, the contemnor, made public allegations of corruption against other judges of the Madras High Court and the Supreme Court.

The contemnor addressed letters containing these allegations to various constitutional functionaries and passed purported judicial orders commanding authorities to take action against the other judges.
The Supreme Court initiated suo motu (on its own initiative) contempt proceedings against the sitting High Court Judge for his conduct.

The contemnor challenged the proceedings, arguing that the Supreme Court had no jurisdiction to initiate contempt against a sitting High Court Judge and that the only legal action available was removal through impeachment.
law: The power to punish for contempt of court is an inherent power of superior courts of record.
The Constitution of India vests the Supreme Court and High Courts with the power to punish for contempt.
This jurisdiction is a special one, not derived from the Contempt of Courts Act, and cannot be taken away by a legislature.
Scandalising the court or interfering with the due course of any judicial proceeding are acts that constitute criminal contempt.
application: The Supreme Court reasoned that it was faced with an "unprecedented situation" resulting from the judge's "incessant questionable conduct."
The Court asserted that there was "no reason to doubt the authority/jurisdiction of this Court to initiate the contempt proceedings."

It explained that if a third party had filed a petition alleging contempt by the judge, the Court would undoubtedly have the jurisdiction to examine it. Therefore, the fact that the proceedings were initiated suo motu by the Court itself makes no difference to their maintainability.

The Court also noted that the contemnor's actions after the proceedings began—such as challenging the Court's jurisdiction and passing his own purported judicial orders—constituted a separate act of criminal contempt by interfering with the due course of justice.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the contemnor's challenge and held that it has the jurisdiction to initiate contempt proceedings against a sitting High Court Judge. The Court affirmed that this authority is based on its inherent power as a superior court of record under the Constitution to punish for acts that scandalize the judiciary and obstruct the administration of justice.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A judge is a dignified person of law who is required to hear both sides of a case and pass an order in accordance with the law.
obiter: There is a need to revisit the process of selection and appointment of judges to the constitutional courts and for all levels of the judiciary.
There is a need to set up an appropriate legal regime to deal with situations like the one in the present case.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Court concluded that despite the unprecedented nature of initiating contempt proceedings against a sitting High Court Judge, it was a necessary step in the administration of justice. The Court reasoned that its fundamental duty is to evaluate controversies based on facts, without fear or favour, and in this process, the identity of the individual is inconsequential. While acknowledging that this was "virgin territory" and a situation that "should never happen," the Court asserted that its constitutional task to administer justice compelled it to proceed against the contemnor regardless of his judicial office.
legal_tests_applied: The court did not apply a formal legal test but rather a foundational principle of judicial duty: that in the process of administration of justice, the individual's identity is clearly inconsequential, and the Court is tasked to evaluate controversies based on the facts of the case, without fear or favour, affection or ill-will.
why_appellant_lost: The challenge to the Court's jurisdiction failed because the Court held that the status of the contemnor as a sitting judge does not provide immunity from contempt proceedings. The Court's reasoning established that its fundamental duty to administer justice and uphold the rule of law is not constrained by the identity or office of the individual involved.
why_respondent_won: The Court's jurisdiction was affirmed based on its inherent and constitutional duty to protect the administration of justice. The Court reasoned that the allegations made by the contemnor were a "serious matter" requiring action "in the interest of both the purity of the judiciary and the constitutional governance of this nation," thereby making the exercise of its contempt jurisdiction not just permissible but necessary.
policy_considerations: The Court considered the action necessary for the "purity of the judiciary and the constitutional governance of this nation."
The case was seen as having "importance extending beyond the immediate problem," highlighting the need to revisit the process of selection and appointment of judges to constitutional courts.
The Court also noted the case highlights "the need to set up appropriate legal regime to deal with" similar situations in the future.
